newsitem.title: USA: U.S. lawmaker Kasich urges early Bosnia pullout.
newsitem.headline: U.S. lawmaker Kasich urges early Bosnia pullout.

text.p: House of Representatives Budget Committee chairman John Kasich said on Sunday he would press for an early end to U.S. participation in NATO's planned follow-on peackeeping force in Bosnia.
Blasting President Bill Clinton's decision to let U.S. troops stay for up to another 18 months as a "big mistake," Kasich said his "sense" was that they should be home by spring.

"We did our job over there. It's now up to the Europeans to exercise real burden-sharing and American forces ought to come home in a timely manner, and soon," he said on the NBC television programme "Meet the Press."

Samuel Berger, Clinton's national security adviser-designate, said in a later television appearance that U.S. troops would stay "roughly" 18 months. "Sooner or later, the parties in Bosnia are going to have to make their own way," he said on the ABC programme "This Week."
After his reelection in November, Clinton acknowledged that Bosnia was not ready for U.S. or other NATO troops to leave on Dec. 20, as originally planned.

Under Clinton's new plan, U.S. forces, originally 20,000, would be reduced to 8,500. Their mission, similar to that of the past year, would be to implement peace accords negotiated in Dayton, Ohio, in November 1995 to end 3-1/2 years of civil war.
Richard Lugar, an Indiana Republican on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, termed the situation in Bosnia "a ticking timebomb of difficulties."

Speaking on "This Week," he said NATO was failing to exercise its authority on a range of tasks. He cited hunting down indicted war criminals, helping restore commerce, returning refugees to their homes, building political legitimacy through local elections and taking control of stockpiled weapons.

Kasich, an Ohio Republican, said he feared the United States was on its way to becoming a permanent military presence in Bosnia, but conceded "we can't get out right now." "My sense is this spring" he added, referring to when U.S. troops should leave.
"I am very concerned this could represent a permanent presence in Bosnia like we've had in Korea" since the 1950-53 Korean War, Kasich said.

"I think it would be a major mistake and I think that the risk to our troops over time is too high and it is not in the vital American interest," he said. "We've done our job. Now we've got to think about coming home and letting them complete the job over there in Europe."
